chapter: Chicago in the 1950s: Mercury, unions and jobbing
title: No solo piano jobs in 1950s Chicago
summary: Hodes explains that solo piano needs a comic patter and no club would pay for it. He had to keep a small band.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: So, back again, to get a band because you have to eat, you've got to work. And there's no solo places in Chicago in the '50s. To play solo, you have to sing, you have to tell jokes. You have to come on with the come-on. I hadn't arrived to where I could talk to audiences anyway. And certainly,

drinking audiences kind of -- I don't know how to handle them too well. Some people know. I've seen one guy turn to the audience, one trumpet player and say to somebody who was getting obnoxious, he says, I don't come on your job and take your broom and shovel away.

And you develop remarks like that, and I wasn't into that. So I decided I better think of something else, the single was out. There was no place where you could play as a single for people to come in and just listen to you. There was no place. I don't know if there's anyplace in Chicago now, that they would pay to hear a single play by himself. And this is the tragedy.
